title: Chethuangni Kothoma
title_english: The Tale of the Chethuang Tree
source_institution: Directorate of Kokborok and Other Minority Languages, Government of Tripura
summary: One of the most revered cautionary folktales of the Borok people, recorded in folkloric collections such as Dr. Jagadis Gan-Choudhury's 'Folk-Tales of Tripura' (1985) and the Centre for Contemporary Folklore archive ('Lightning, Thunder and the Chethuang Tree'). It tells the story of a young maiden who flees an unlawful familial advance by seeking refuge at a sacred Chethuang tree (Alstonia scholaris). As she pleads with the tree, it rises miraculously into the sky to protect her dignity. The myth provides an etiology for why the Chethuang tree has a flat canopy without an apical shoot and associates lightning and thunder with ancestral remembrance.
content:
In traditional Borok lore of the Tripura hills, a brother and sister embarked on a journey across the ridge forests. Before their journey, elders had warned them of respecting natural taboos and ancestral moral boundaries. While crossing a stream, the sister lifted her rignai to keep it dry, which stirred an unlawful infatuation in the brother, violating the sacred clan code of exogamy.

Fleeing in distress to protect her virtue and clan dignity, the maiden ran into the deep forest and sought refuge at the trunk of a Chethuang tree (Alstonia scholaris). Weeping, she pleaded with the tree to grow upward to the heavens. The tree answered her prayers, growing steadily skyward until it pierced the canopy and carried her beyond reach into the sky.

According to Tripuri oral tradition, this legend explains why the Chethuang tree naturally spreads flat at its crown without a central apical shoot. In folklore, flashes of lightning on stormy days are likened to the maiden's spirit in the clouds, and the rumbling of thunder echoes the strikes of axes when her kin attempted in vain to bring the tree down.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Gan-Choudhury, Jagadis (1985). 'Folk-Tales of Tripura'. Directorate of Higher Education, Govt. of Tripura.

title: Khumpui Kothoma (Raima bai Saima)
title_english: The Legend of the Khumpui Flower
source_institution: Tribal Research and Cultural Institute (TRCI), Government of Tripura
summary: Traditional sacred legend of the sisters Raima and Saima and the white fragrant Khumpui blossom (Hedychium coronarium). Documented in ethnographic collections including Dr. Jagadis Gan-Choudhury's 'Folk-Tales of Tripura' (1985) and TRCI oral archives. The tale accounts for the sacred origin of the Gomati River and the pilgrimage falls at Dumbur.
content:
In traditional Tripuri oral heritage, two devoted sisters, Raima and Saima, lived in the river valleys of eastern Tripura. Their lives were bound to jhum farming, hillside weaving, and the wild floral streams. Through divine transformation linked to an enchanted serpent-spirit and sacred water tests, their steadfast bond gave rise to the rivers Raima and Sarma, which join to form the holy Gomati River.

Where Raima walked in devotion, the delicate, snow-white Khumpui blossom (Hedychium coronarium) bloomed along the river cliffs. In traditional folklore, the blossom is a touchstone of innocence and fidelity, blooming pure when touched by truthful hands and withering before deceit. The waterfalls of Dumbur remain a sacred pilgrimage site during Pous Sankranti, where the legend continues to be remembered.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Gan-Choudhury, Jagadis (1985). 'Folk-Tales of Tripura'. Directorate of Higher Education, Govt. of Tripura.

title: Nuwai Tokni Kothoma
title_english: The Tale of the Nuwai Birds and the Two Sisters
source_institution: Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council (TTAADC)
summary: One of the most famous and widely recorded folk stories across the Borok communities of Tripura, featured in Dr. Jagadis Gan-Choudhury's 'Folk-Tales of Tripura' (1985) and the 'Kwtham Kothoma' indigenous storytelling projects. It contrasts jealousy, cruelty, and maternal favoritism with kindness, patience, and transformation into the calling Nuwai birds.
content:
In a hillside village lived two sisters under the care of their family. One daughter was gentle and dutiful, carrying out her chores on the jhum slopes with patience, while the other was self-indulgent and envious. When the gentle sister was subjected to harsh trials in the forest by an unkind stepmother, forest spirits and birds offered her shelter and nourishment in return for her humble kindness.

When the envious sister attempted to demand identical gifts through pride and malice, she met with misadventure and shame. The narrative concludes with the transformation of the sisters into the forest birds known in Kokborok as Nuwai, whose dual calls across the ridge valleys serve as a perennial reminder in Borok villages of the enduring rewards of gentle humility.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Gan-Choudhury, Jagadis (1985). 'Folk-Tales of Tripura'. Directorate of Higher Education, Govt. of Tripura, pp. 24-29.

title: Kuchuk Kherengbar
title_english: The Tale of the Scentless Kherengbar Flower
source_institution: Tribal Research and Cultural Institute (TRCI), Government of Tripura
summary: Classic Tripuri etiological folktale explaining the origins of the Kherengbar flower, documenting how a heavenly blossom was stripped of its fragrance due to a sorrowful romantic transgression. Documented in 'Kwtham Kothoma' indigenous lore collections.
content: According to ancient Tripuri mythology, Kherengbar was originally a flower of ethereal beauty and celestial fragrance that grew only in the garden of the divine realm. When a youth from earth ascended the hills and brought the blossom down to present to his beloved in defiance of divine warnings, the flower retained its striking crimson and orange petals but was stripped forever of its sweet scent by divine decree. The story explains why the vivid Kherengbar blooms brightly across the hill slopes of Tripura without perfume.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: TRCI Folklore Archives, Government of Tripura; 'Kwtham Kothoma' Cultural Project.

title: Baba Gariani Kothoma
title_english: The Legend of Baba Garia and Hojagiri
source_institution: Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council (TTAADC)
summary: The sacred mythological lore of Lord Garia, the guardian deity of livestock, household prosperity, and abundant harvest, worshipped during Garia Puja at the conclusion of Chaitra Sankranti and the opening days of Buisu (Tripuri New Year). Accompanied by the sacred Hojagiri and Garia dances.
content:
Baba Garia is worshipped as the supreme benefactor of fertility, livestock, and agricultural bounty across all Borok clans. Legend recounts that Baba Garia visits every village during the turn of the new year, riding upon auspicious spirits to inspect household granaries and fields.

A ceremonial bamboo pole adorned with wild cotton garlands, threaded rice, and floral offerings is carried from house to house by the youth. The households welcome Garia with rice beer, cooked grains, and prayers. The sacred Hojagiri and Garia dances, with their balancing on earthen pots and brass platters, enact the divine balance of nature and celebrate communal solidarity.

metadata.sacred_symbol: Adorned bamboo pole of Baba Garia

title: Subrai Rajani Kothoma
title_english: The Myth of Subrai Raja
source_institution: Directorate of Kokborok and Other Minority Languages, Government of Tripura
summary: Primordial culture hero and mythic sovereign in Borok cosmology, remembered through oral incantations recited by traditional Ojhas (priests and medicinal healers). Subrai established social laws, matrimonial conventions, and the veneration of protective deities.
content:
In early Borok oral cosmology, Subrai Raja is remembered as the foundational culture sovereign who organized society in the hill ranges of eastern India. Guided by the spiritual forces of the fourteen ancestral protector spirits, Subrai established the customary rites of childbirth, marriage rites, jhum boundaries, and seasonal thanksgiving.

Chants passed down through the Ojhas invoke Subrai as the primal custodian of law who taught humankind how to live in equilibrium with forest spirits and river streams. His memory forms the spiritual backdrop to traditional Tripuri customary law.

title: Kokborok Kokbwkrai (Proverbs and Sayings)
title_english: Traditional Kokborok Proverbs and Philosophical Sayings
author_or_source: Traditional Tripuri Oral Literature / Academic Field Studies
source_institution: IOSR Journal of Humanities and Social Science (IOSR-JHSS)
summary: Authentic Kokborok proverbs (Kokbwkrai / Kok-hajakma) documented and verified in peer-reviewed academic linguistic literature by Faijul Hoque in 'Kokborok: A Major Tribal Language of Tripura' (IOSR-JHSS, 2014). Illustrates traditional Tripuri moral ethics and philosophical insights.
content:
1. Dangai pho bokha bising kabo.
   Literal: Even while suffering, the heart weeps inside.
   Meaning: Sufferers can truly realize the sorrows of others.

2. Beng-nog beng nango.
   Literal: One who digs a pit for others falls into it.
   Meaning: Those who plot harm against others fall into their own traps.

3. Siyari bai twima ongia.
   Literal: Fog alone cannot create a river.
   Meaning: Superficial appearances cannot substitute for substance and truth.

4. Sa haya hai bithi rukh.
   Literal: Administering medicine according to the disease.
   Meaning: Apply the appropriate remedy tailored to the specific problem.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Hoque, Faijul (2014). 'Kokborok: A Major Tribal Language of Tripura'. IOSR Journal of Humanities and Social Science (IOSR-JHSS), Vol. 19, Issue 10, Ver. V, pp. 30-35.

title: Uayingkhilimung (Traditional Kokborok Lullaby)
title_english: Traditional Kokborok Cradle Lullaby
author_or_source: Traditional Borok Oral Folk Poetry (Luku Rwchabmung)
source_institution: Directorate of Kokborok and Other Minority Languages, Government of Tripura
summary: Authentic traditional cradle lullaby (Uayingkhilimung) collected from Kokborok oral literature. Sung by mothers and grandmothers to rock infants to sleep, referencing parental roles and traditional royalty in lyrical rhyme.
content:
O……le…le…le…..,
Rangchakni bupha twiwi,
Nwphabo thungkha Rajani seboki,
Nwmabo thungkha Rajani daijwk.
O……

English Translation:
O... gentle child, sleep,
Bearing the golden blossom,
Your father has gone to serve as the King's guard,
Your mother attends at the royal loom.
O... sleep in peace.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Documented in Kokborok oral verbal art archives (Directorate of Kokborok & Other Minority Languages).

title: Mamita Rwchapmung (Jhum Harvest Song)
title_english: Mamita Harvest Festival Folk Song
source_institution: Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council (TTAADC)
summary: Authentic traditional verse from Mamita Rwchapmung, performed during the autumn post-harvest celebrations welcoming the new paddy (mai kwtal) into village granaries.
content:
Da kwtal twiwi Ri-kwtal kanwi,
Sarikpang ochai hwnwi,
Nokhwla pharwi nokhwla sibwi,
Bisi bisini khali khalini,
Kangal Mamita rio.

English Translation:
Holding the new harvest sickle, wearing the newly woven cloth,
Calling upon the respected village elder and priest,
Sweeping clean the courtyard, beautifying the compound,
Year after year through every season,
We welcome the joyous Mamita festival.

metadata.bibliographic_citation: Documented in ethnographic studies of Tripuri jhum harvest culture and oral songs.

title: Kokborma (Tripura-Byakaran)
title_english: Kokborma (Earliest Printed Grammar of Tripuri)
source_institution: Amar Jantra, Comilla / Historical Linguistic Archives
summary: Historically recognized as the earliest printed grammar primer of the Tripuri language, printed at Amar Jantra in Comilla in 1897. It is historically notable as the earliest documented printed text where an early written form of the language name appeared in print.

title: Kok-Borok-Ma (First Grammar by a Royal Tripuri Scholar)
title_english: Kok-Borok-Ma (Pioneering Kokborok Grammar)
source_institution: Royal State Press, Agartala / National Library of India
summary: Monumental milestone in Kokborok linguistic history. Published in 1900 at Agartala under the patronship of Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya, 'Kok-Borok-Ma' was authored by royal scholar Thakur Radhamohan Debbarma. It was the first book to formally standardize and popularize the exact term 'Kokborok' in print, providing an extensive grammatical analysis of word roots, suffixes, and nominal prefixes.

title: Traipur Kothamala
title_english: Tripuri Phrases and Conversational Guide
source_institution: Royal State Press, Agartala / Tripura State Archives
summary: Published in 1906 by Thakur Radhamohan Debbarma as a follow-up to Kok-Borok-Ma. A pioneering trilingual conversational phrasebook (Kokborok, Bengali, English) designed to facilitate administration, education, and social dialogue in the princely state of Tripura.

title: Traipur Bhasabidhan
title_english: Tripuri Language Lexicon
source_institution: Royal State Press, Agartala / State Central Library Agartala
summary: Published in 1907 as a vocabulary companion to Kok-Borok-Ma, documenting botanical classifications, agricultural tools, clan titles, and traditional lexicon of the Borok language.

title: Rajmala (Royal Chronicle of Tripura)
title_english: The Chronicle of the Kings of Tripura
author_or_source: Compiled by Royal Chroniclers (Durlabhendra, Sukreshwar, Baneshwar)
source_institution: Asiatic Society of Bengal & Directorate of Higher Education Tripura
summary: The monumental verse chronicle commissioned by Maharaja Dharma Manikya. It records the oral lineages, migrations, and spiritual rites of the Tripuri monarchs and the Fourteen Gods (Choddodevata), drawing on ancient Kokborok oral chants preserved by the royal Chantai (head priest). Later critical edition edited by Kaliprasanna Sen (1926-1931).

title: Kokborok Grammar
title_english: Kokborok Grammar (CIIL Descriptive Grammar)
source_institution: Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), Mysore
summary: Landmark 20th-century descriptive linguistic grammar published by the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), Government of India, in 1976. Authored by linguist Pushpa Pai, it provided the first modern structural linguistic description of Kokborok phonology, morphological inflections, and syntax.

metadata.publisher: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore

title: Haping Garingo Chibuksa Ringo
title_english: The Snake Calls in the Low Hills
source_institution: Sahitya Akademi & Kokborok Sahitya Sanskriti Samsad
summary: Landmark modern Kokborok poetry collection published in 1987 by Kokborok Sahitya Sanskriti Samsad (Agartala), edited by Shyamlal Debbarma. In 1996, Chandrakanta Murasingh received the inaugural Sahitya Akademi Bhasha Samman for this and his poetic contributions portraying indigenous identity, sorrow, and resistance in the Tripura hills.

title: Holong Kok Sa-o Bolong Bisingo
title_english: The Stone Speaks in the Forest
source_institution: Sahitya Akademi & Akshar Publications, Agartala
summary: Poetry collection by Chandrakanta Murasingh published in 1995, featuring poignant reflections on environmental sanctity, forest ecology, militarization, and indigenous grief in contemporary Tripura.

title: Karachi theke Longtharai
title_english: From Karachi to Longtharai (Novel / Film Longtharai)
source_institution: Agartala Book Bureau & Directorate of Kokborok, Tripura
summary: Acclaimed novel by writer and legislator Bimal Sinha depicting tribal resilience and social realities along the Longtharai hills of Tripura. Served as the literary basis for 'Longtharai' (1986), the historic first-ever feature film in the Kokborok language, directed by Dipak Bhattacharya.

metadata.cinematic_adaptation: Adapted into the first Kokborok feature film 'Longtharai' (1986, dir. Dipak Bhattacharya)

title: Hor Diporo Rwchapmung
title_english: The Midnight Song
source_institution: Sahitya Akademi & Kokborok Sahitya Sabha
summary: Poetry collection by Shefali Debbarma, one of the leading feminine voices in modern Kokborok literature. Debbarma received the Tripura State Award for Poetry in 2004; her critically acclaimed poem 'Lamination' (exploring indigenous identity) was selected for the '100 Great Indian Poems' anthology edited by Abhay K.

title: Anglo-Kokborok Dictionary
title_english: English-Kokborok Dictionary
source_institution: Kokborok Sahitya Sabha & TTAADC
summary: Standard lexicographical reference compiled by Binoy Debbarma, first published in 1993 (revised edition 2002) under Kokborok Sahitya Sabha and TTAADC. Widely utilized in educational institutions and linguistic research across Tripura.
